To aggregate means to gather many separate things and bring them together into one combined whole or total.

That's the heart of it.
A picture to make it click

Imagine 1,000 people fill out a customer satisfaction survey. Each person gives their own individual rating. Now, a company takes all 1,000 of those separate ratings and pulls them into one place to analyze them together. That act — of collecting all those scattered individual pieces and combining them into one unified dataset — is aggregating.

The separate pieces don't disappear or melt into each other. They're still individual items. But now they are being treated and handled as one collective whole.
What makes "aggregate" different from just "collect" or "gather"?

This is the important part.

When you collect things, you simply pick them up or put them in one place. It's neutral. No particular purpose is implied.

When you aggregate things, there's a specific intent: you're bringing them together so that the combined result is what matters — the total, the sum, the overall picture. The emphasis is on what the whole adds up to.

Think of it this way:

  • A child collects seashells → she picks them up and puts them in a bucket. That's it.
  • A scientist aggregates water samples from 50 rivers → she pulls them all together specifically to study them as a combined dataset and find patterns.

The word "aggregate" implies purposeful, systematic gathering aimed at producing a unified whole that can be studied, reported, or acted upon.

These examples cover different situations where the word naturally appears:

  • "The app aggregates your spending data from all your bank accounts into one dashboard." → It pulls together all the separate transactions from different accounts so you see one complete financial picture.
  • "The news website aggregates articles from hundreds of sources." → It collects articles from all over the internet and presents them in one place.
  • "Researchers aggregated results from 30 different studies to reach a stronger conclusion." → They combined the findings from each individual study to analyze them as a whole, making the conclusion more powerful than any single study could.
  • "The platform aggregates customer reviews from across the web." → It gathers reviews from many different websites and brings them together.
  • "The government aggregated employment data from all 50 states." → It compiled the data from every state into one national figure.
The passive form — you'll see this a lot

Very often, you'll encounter "aggregate" in the passive voice:

  • "The data was aggregated from multiple sources."
  • "Survey responses were aggregated and analyzed."

This just means someone (or a system) performed the action of gathering and combining — but the focus is on the result, not on who did it. Don't let the passive form confuse you; the meaning is the same.
What kinds of things get aggregated?

This is a useful pattern to notice: you almost always aggregate things that are informational, numerical, or measurable — things that, once combined, can be analyzed or summarized. Common examples:

  • Data
  • Statistics
  • Results
  • Scores
  • Feedback
  • Opinions
  • Information
  • Content (like news articles or reviews)

You wouldn't typically say "I aggregated the chairs in the room." The word lives primarily in the world of information, numbers, and analysis. When there is a lot of it, coming from many different sources, and someone needs to pull it together to make sense of it — that's when "aggregate" appears.
Register and tone — when is this word used?

"Aggregate" as a verb is moderately formal. You'll encounter it most in:

  • Technology and data science ("The system aggregates user behavior.")
  • Business and finance ("We aggregate sales figures quarterly.")
  • Research and academia ("The meta-analysis aggregated data from 50 trials.")
  • Journalism and media ("The site aggregates content from thousands of publishers.")

In casual everyday speech, people tend to say "combine," "pool together," "compile," or "gather" instead. But those words don't carry the same precision. "Aggregate" specifically signals that you're pulling many separate pieces into a unified whole — with the purpose of seeing what the collection amounts to or represents as a total.
The one-sentence summary to lock it in
To aggregate is to systematically bring together many separate things — especially data, information, or results — so that they can be treated, analyzed, or presented as a single combined whole.
